prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, and their development to the 10^-18 level, opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 alone, with Katori and Ye. After the first round all eight of us stand on the same part, which I treat as a coincidence of independent judgments and not as evidence in itself. What carries the case for me is the physics. Trapping thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, so that the lattice light shifts the two clock levels equally, is a distinct principle; it is what turned statistical power and systematic control into a 10^-18 clock. Nature has then checked the result for us: clocks in different laboratories and countries agree, a gravitational redshift is resolved over a millimetre-scale sample, and the same clocks now bound drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. That is a clue from nature, not an elegant idea awaiting confirmation. The credit is concentrated: the magic-wavelength proposal and first realisation sit with Katori, and the road to record accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics with Ye. I would word the citation around the lattice concept so that it claims neither optical clocks in general (2005 comb, 2012 ion control) nor precision for its own sake.
statement.case_against: The objection that survives round 1 is that a lattice clock may be read as a refinement of work already honoured in 2005 and 2012. I think the distinctness argument holds, and that the colleagues in atomic physics, Lindroth above all, have made it better than I did in my own opening. The weaker flank is attribution. Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the SYRTE, NIST and PTB groups made decisive contributions, and a two-name credit leaves them out. This is a real cost, but the Nobel rules and the three-person cap oblige us to choose, and I cannot identify a third person whose claim to the lattice concept or its first realisation is clearly on par. Olsson's point that 10^-18 is a record in systematic control, not a discovery, is also fair; it is the reason I want the citation to carry the consequences for tests of fundamental physics, not only the number.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the comb and ion-trap prizes honoured tools and control of single systems, whereas the magic wavelength lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, and that millimetre time dilation is a new observation about nature.
responses.response: I accept that and have moved from worry to confidence on the overlap question; as a string theorist I defer to you on atomic structure. My follow-up request, as Secretary, is concrete: since you work close to this field, please state whether the first strontium lattice clock and the early magic-wavelength proposals sit with Katori in the way our statements assume. If an external expert report would contradict that, I want to hear it before the vote. On B042 I remain where I was: the choice of three among five founders would be a decision about priority that the literature has not made for us.

responses.point: Olsson fears that the headline 10^-18 result is a matter of systematic uncertainty, closer to a record than a discovery, and keeps B015 (tunnelling magnetoresistance) as a serious alternative, with the 1995 Miyazaki and Moodera experiments as the original discovery.
responses.response: I agree that a record is not a discovery, and I would resist a citation that rests on the number alone. What makes B001 a discovery in my view is what the number revealed: a redshift across a millimetre, tests of constants and dark matter that were out of reach before, and many-body physics inside the clock itself. On B015, I respect the thirty years of confirmation and the industrial use. But you yourself and Kroll, Mehlig and Pearce show that the credit splits between the 1995 room-temperature step and the MgO step, with Yuasa, Djayaprawira, Butler and Mathon outside the names. Until the committee decides which step it honours, I cannot place it ahead of a case where proposal and realisation sit with the same two people. I have not added it to my alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll holds that waiting for the SI second redefinition would reward a bureaucratic milestone, not the physics, and asks whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would improve the configuration or only dilute it.
responses.response: We agree on timing, and I would put it more sharply: the redefinition is a decision that follows from the discovery, so a prize that waited for it would make us hostage to a process we do not control. On the second part I side with your caution. Adding B042 would bring in the five-name problem and add a second atomic-optical result to a field that has already been honoured several times; adding B003 would collide with last year's circuit prize, and Johansson himself would have to step aside. A second part is justified only if it is clearly mature and cleanly credited, and nothing on the list meets both tests this year. I have therefore changed my alternatives to B042 and B017, dropping B045.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B010 (topological insulators) to B001, and worries that this shift may reflect a wish for consensus more than his own judgment of merit; he keeps B010 and B017 as alternatives.
responses.response: I think the self-check you describe is exactly the right one, and your answer that the attribution is cleaner than in any condensed-matter candidate on the list is a scientific reason, not social pressure. I share your hesitation on B017: the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle graphene is solid, but until the pairing mechanism is clearer I would wait. I keep it as an alternative because the platform has opened phenomena that were inaccessible, which is the kind of tool I normally value. Please do not drop your own judgment on topological insulators for later years; I would simply want the credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal to be resolved by an external report before it comes to a vote.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, wants the citation worded around the lattice clock concept and the 10^-18 demonstration, and agrees that other groups are the real exposure of the attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the wording, and have adopted it above: the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice and its development to 10^-18, with new tests of fundamental physics as the consequence. As for the exposure, I would not try to repair it by adding a name. A third laureate chosen from the Paris, NIST or PTB teams would be an arbitrary cut, and the citation can instead describe the concept and its realisation so that the public record shows the field was larger than the two people. I would still ask that we agree to put this in writing in the deliberation record so that the exposure is stated openly, not hidden.

uncertainties: Whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium realisation precede, in the way our statements assume, the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and the other groups; I rely on colleagues' recollection and would want an external expert report to confirm the priority record before the vote.
Whether a majority will accept lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, even though every round-1 statement argues that they are.
Whether a two-name credit for B001 will be seen as fair by the wider clock community, since the three-person cap prevents any wider recognition.
Whether B042 or B017 could mature quickly enough, through a clearer split of credit or a resolved pairing mechanism, to make a second part sensible in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B042 or B017. My Uppsala string-theory background, my supervisor David Gross and my collaborator Thomas Van Riet have no link to any candidate named on the shortlist. As Secretary I have a procedural interest in external reports on the priority record, but this gives me no stake in any candidate.
